headline: High Court sets verdict date today in child Achiya rape and murder case
summary: The High Court today set the date for its verdict on the death reference and appeal of the main accused in the rape and murder of 8-year-old Achiya from Magura, following the conclusion of hearings.
details: The High Court today set the date for its verdict in the rape and murder case of eight-year-old Achiya from Magura. The hearing on the death reference and appeal of the accused, Hitu Sheikh, concluded yesterday.
A bench comprising Justice Bhishmadev Chakraborty and Justice K M Rasheduzzaman Raja concluded the hearing today, August 25, and set the date for the pronouncement of the judgment.
Previously, the state-appointed lawyer conducted an expedited hearing on the death reference and appeal filed by Hitu Sheikh, who was sentenced to death by a lower court.
On May 17, 2025, the judge of the Magura Women and Child Repression Prevention Tribunal, M Zahid Hasan, sentenced the primary accused to death. Three other defendants in the case were acquitted.

Achiya was subjected to torture in March 2025 while visiting her sister-in-law's house in Nij Nanduayali village, Magura. She was initially admitted to hospitals in Magura and Faridpur in critical condition.
Subsequently, she was transferred to Dhaka Medical College Hospital and then to Dhaka's Combined Military Hospital. Achiya tragically passed away on March 13 while receiving treatment there.
caption:
The High Court today set the verdict date in the tragic rape and murder case of 8-year-old Achiya. This case has drawn national attention since 2025.

The High Court today set the date for its verdict in the rape and murder case of eight-year-old Achiya from Magura. The hearing on the death reference and appeal of the accused, Hitu Sheikh, concluded yesterday.

A bench comprising Justice Bhishmadev Chakraborty and Justice K M Rasheduzzaman Raja concluded the hearing today, August 25, and set the date for the pronouncement of the judgment.

Previously, the state-appointed lawyer conducted an expedited hearing on the death reference and appeal filed by Hitu Sheikh, who was sentenced to death by a lower court.

On May 17, 2025, the judge of the Magura Women and Child Repression Prevention Tribunal, M Zahid Hasan, sentenced the primary accused to death. Three other defendants in the case were acquitted.

Achiya was subjected to torture in March 2025 while visiting her sister-in-law's house in Nij Nanduayali village, Magura. She was initially admitted to hospitals in Magura and Faridpur in critical condition.

Subsequently, she was transferred to Dhaka Medical College Hospital and then to Dhaka's Combined Military Hospital. Achiya tragically passed away on March 13 while receiving treatment there.

headline: 7 lakh students fail in SSC & equivalent exams, lowest pass rate in two decades
summary: Nearly 700,000 students failed this year's SSC and equivalent exams, marking the lowest pass rate in two decades and exposing deep-seated issues within the national education system.
details: Approximately 700,000 students failed the recent SSC and equivalent examinations, representing a 35-40% dropout rate. This alarming result, the lowest pass rate in two decades, highlights a severe crisis within Bangladesh's education system.

The failure is attributed to a collective responsibility involving students, families, teachers, and education administration. A shocking 312 educational institutions reported zero passes, indicating systemic issues.

Weaknesses in English and Mathematics led to over half of humanities students failing. The lack of basic literacy and numeracy skills among millions of students even after reaching secondary levels points to a deeper problem than simple accountability.

A 2024 World Bank analysis on 'Learning Poverty' reveals that 51% of Bangladeshi children completing primary school lack the basic comprehension skills for their age-appropriate texts. While education access has expanded, quality has severely lagged.

The current system is criticized for being exam-oriented, prioritizing rote learning over critical thinking, logical analysis, and practical application of knowledge. This outdated approach is seen as 'stealing the future' of students, as noted by John Dewey.

Recent social degradation, post-'July Revolution' psychological trauma, and general instability have exacerbated these long-standing structural weaknesses. Students' disengagement due to these factors also contributes to the problem.

Teachers also face extreme frustration and a lack of professional development, stemming from inadequate education budgets and prolonged neglect. This has created a void of professional commitment within educational institutions.

The state must urgently assess the immense economic loss caused by this failure, equating to billions or trillions of dollars in national damage over the long term. Solutions like Finland's continuous assessment and China's industry-linked technical education are suggested.

To build a world-class generation, Bangladesh needs a work-oriented education model supported by sufficient funding. The current allocation of only around 2% of GDP to education is insufficient for teacher development, technological advancement, and effective vocational training.

This year's 700,000 failed students serve as a stark warning. The government's immediate priority should be to guide these students towards alternative vocational paths or reintegrate them into the mainstream through positive motivation, ensuring public exams are not a dead end but a gateway to new opportunities.
